title: How to empty the trash in Finder on Mac: steps, shortcuts and fixes
metaTitle: How to Empty the Trash in Finder on Mac (Step by Step)
description: How to empty the trash in Finder on Mac: click Empty or press ⇧⌘⌫, confirm the warning, skip it with Option, and fix a Trash that stalls.

intro: To empty the trash in Finder on Mac, click the Trash icon in the Dock, then click Empty in the upper-right corner of the Trash window. Confirm with Empty Trash in the warning dialog, or press ⇧⌘⌫ to start the same process from the keyboard.
tldr: Click the Trash icon in the Dock, click Empty, then click Empty Trash in the warning dialog.
Or choose Finder > Empty Trash, or press ⇧⌘⌫ (Shift-Command-Delete) with Finder active.
Press ⌥⇧⌘⌫ to empty without the warning, or turn the warning off in Finder > Settings > Advanced.
To remove one item for good, Control-click it in the Trash, choose Delete Immediately, then click Delete.
If the Trash stalls on a progress bar, click the X at the end of the bar, then restart if it still hangs.

blocks.text: Emptying the Trash is the last step of deleting a file on a Mac. Until you empty it, the item stays in the Trash, and you can still drag it back. Once you empty it, Finder removes the items from your Mac. That is why this page covers the warning, the shortcuts, and the few cases where the Trash misbehaves.
Empty the Trash from the Dock

Start with the Dock method. It is the one most people use, and it shows you what is inside before anything goes. Click the Trash icon at the far right of the Dock. The Trash window opens and lists every item you have deleted and not yet emptied. Scroll the list first. If something there still matters, drag it back to where it belongs before you go further.

Next, click Empty in the upper-right corner of the Trash window. Finder shows a warning dialog. Click Empty Trash to confirm. While the Trash works through its contents, Finder shows an Emptying the Trash window with a progress bar. Leave it alone until it finishes.

Treat the list as a final check, not a formality. Look for folders with names you do not recognize, because they may hold work you forgot about. Open them, look inside, and decide before you press anything. Once the empty runs, you cannot pick individual items back out.
Use the Finder menu instead

If the Dock is hidden, or you prefer menus, use Finder. Click the Finder icon in the Dock, or click an empty part of the desktop, so Finder is the active app. Then choose Finder > Empty Trash from the menu bar at the top of the screen. You get the same warning dialog and the same Empty Trash button. The result is identical.

The menu route suits people who keep their hands on the trackpad. It also helps when the Dock is hidden and the Trash icon is out of reach. Pick the route that feels quickest. Apple lists both as valid ways to empty the Trash, so neither one is the correct choice.
The keyboard shortcut and the Option trick

The fastest route is the keyboard. Press Shift-Command-Delete (⇧⌘⌫) with Finder active. Apple's keyboard shortcut list says this empties the Trash. Add Option to skip the dialog. Option-Shift-Command-Delete (⌥⇧⌘⌫) empties the Trash without a confirmation.

Apple's shortcut list does not say whether plain ⇧⌘⌫ shows the dialog. Only the Option version is described as skipping it. The first time you use the shortcut, watch the screen so you know what your Mac does. Holding Option while you click Empty, or while you choose Empty Trash, also skips the warning once.

blocks.caption: How each method empties the Trash, based on Apple's steps

blocks.text: Think of Option as the switch that skips the dialog. It works on the keyboard shortcut, and it works on the Empty button and the Finder menu too. Without Option, the warning stays in place.
Which method to pick

Pick the method that fits your hands. Use the Dock when you want to look at the list first. Use ⇧⌘⌫ when you keep your hands on the keyboard and trust the dialog to catch mistakes. Use ⌥⇧⌘⌫ only for a cleanup you have already checked. The result is the same in each case. The only difference is how much you see before the items go.

If you are not sure, keep the warning on for a while. Empty with the Dock method and read each dialog. If you never needed the dialog to stop a mistake, you can switch to a faster route later. If it did catch one, keep the pause.
Turn the warning off, or skip it once

The warning is a useful pause, and it is on by default. If you empty the Trash often and feel sure of your habits, you can turn it off. Choose Finder > Settings, click Advanced, and deselect Show warning before emptying the Trash. From then on, Empty removes the items straight away.

Turning it off has a cost. You lose the last chance to catch a mistake, and a full Trash can go in one click. If you only want the warning gone once, hold Option while you click Empty instead. The next normal empty asks again.

blocks.title: Check before you empty
blocks.text: Emptying the Trash removes its items from your Mac. Look through the list first, then empty it. Keep the warning on until you know your own habits.
Delete one item from the Trash

Sometimes you want one file gone and the rest kept. Open the Trash, then Control-click the item. Choose Delete Immediately from the menu. Click Delete in the warning. Only that item goes. The others stay in the Trash until you empty it, or until the 30-day setting removes them if you turned that on.

Here is a common case. A large installer sits in the Trash next to photos you still want. Control-click the installer, choose Delete Immediately, then click Delete. The photos stay in the Trash, and you can empty them later with any method above.
Let macOS empty the Trash on its own

You can skip manual emptying. Choose Finder > Settings, click Advanced, and tick Remove items from the Trash after 30 days. Finder then deletes trashed items after 30 days. Items from iCloud Drive follow a stricter rule. They are always emptied after 30 days, whatever this setting says.

Take a file you move to the Trash on the first day of the month. With the setting on, Finder removes it 30 days later, unless you empty the Trash sooner. Auto-clean suits people who forget to empty. It fits poorly if you use the Trash as a safety net for a week-long project.
Pick the rule that matches how you work, and check the setting once so you know it is there.
Why check the Trash first

Accidental deletion is common. In a 2024 survey by Backblaze, a backup company, 74% of Americans who own a computer said they had accidentally deleted important data. The survey sampled 2,058 U.S. adults, of whom 1,877 own a computer. The Harris Poll fielded it from April 25 to 29, 2024.

Be clear about what that number measures. It asked about important data in general, not about the Trash. It cannot tell you how often people empty the Trash by mistake. It is still a fair reason to scan the list before you press Empty.
A scan costs only a few seconds. Recovering a file you emptied can cost far more, and you may not have a backup ready.
Fix a Trash that won't empty on Mac

The most common complaint is a progress bar that never finishes. In one Apple Community thread, a macOS 13.1 Ventura user saw an Emptying the Trash window stuck on an indeterminate bar. The poster said clicking the X at the end of the bar, labeled Stop Emptying the Trash, emptied the Trash. Another user said that did not work for them, so treat it as one report.

Reports from macOS Tahoe 26 also describe a Trash that does not empty. They come from Apple Community and third-party sites. Apple has not published a Tahoe-specific note on the cause. In one reported case, a restart fixed the problem, so restart first and then try again.
Work through these checks in order, starting with the cheapest one.

items: Watch the Emptying the Trash window for a while before you act.
If the progress bar never moves, click the X at the end of the bar, labeled Stop Emptying the Trash.
If the Trash still will not empty, restart the Mac, then open the Trash and try again.
If you turned the warning off, enable it, empty, then turn it off again. One user reported this workaround. Another said it did not help.

blocks.text: What to do with Recovered Files

After a restart, macOS can place Recovered Files folders in the Trash. Apple advises you to drag out anything useful before you empty the Trash. Do not assume a Recovered Files folder is junk. Open each one, check the contents, and move the keepers to their proper home. Then empty the Trash with Empty or Finder > Empty Trash, and confirm with Empty Trash.
iCloud Drive files work differently

Finder's Trash is a Mac feature. If your files live in iCloud Drive, the web equivalent is the Recently Deleted sidebar at icloud.com/iclouddrive. Select files there to recover them, or select them and choose Delete. You can also choose Delete All. Apple says deleted files can be removed permanently within the 30-day window.
Plan for two clocks. A file in your Mac Trash follows your Finder setting. A file from iCloud Drive follows the iCloud rule, which is always 30 days.
Mistakes people make with the Trash

items: Emptying with the warning turned off, then finding the wrong file gone.
Assuming iCloud Drive files follow your Mac's 30-day setting. They follow the iCloud rule.
Deleting Recovered Files without opening them after a restart.
Expecting plain ⇧⌘⌫ to skip the dialog. Apple documents only the Option version as skipping it.
Emptying the whole Trash when one item needed Delete Immediately.

blocks.text: Next steps

Once the Trash is under control, the next habit is checking files before you delete them. Read [how to use the preview pane in Finder](/how-to/use-the-preview-pane-in-finder) to look at a file's contents first. If you dig through folders often, [show the path bar](/how-to/show-the-path-bar-in-finder) so you can see where each file lives. To keep track of files you want to keep, [add a tag to a file in Finder](/how-to/add-a-tag-to-a-file-in-finder).

If you want to test a few of these steps first, make a folder with two dummy files. Move them to the Trash, then practice the Dock method and the Delete Immediately method. Empty only when you are sure.

faq.question: Does emptying the Trash delete files for good?
faq.answer: Yes. Emptying removes the items from the Trash, and Finder asks you to confirm first unless you turned that warning off. Apple's Trash steps do not describe a way to get items back after you empty the Trash, so check the list before you press Empty.

faq.question: How do I empty the Trash without the warning?
faq.answer: Hold Option while you click Empty or choose Empty Trash to skip the warning once. Press Option-Shift-Command-Delete (⌥⇧⌘⌫) to skip it each time you use that shortcut. To turn the warning off for good, use Finder > Settings > Advanced.

faq.question: How do I delete just one file from the Trash?
faq.answer: Control-click the item in the Trash window, choose Delete Immediately, then click Delete in the warning. Only that item is removed. The rest of the Trash stays as it was.

faq.question: Why is my Trash not emptying on macOS Tahoe?
faq.answer: Community reports describe this on Tahoe 26, and Apple has not published a note on the cause. Restart the Mac and try again. If the progress bar hangs, click the X at the end of it.

faq.question: Does the Trash empty itself?
faq.answer: Only if you tick Remove items from the Trash after 30 days in Finder > Settings > Advanced. iCloud Drive items are always emptied after 30 days, whatever that setting says.

faq.question: Can I get back files I emptied from the Trash?
faq.answer: Apple's pages on the Trash do not describe recovery after you empty it. If you back up your Mac, check that backup before you assume the file is gone for good.

troubleshooting.problem: The Trash progress bar never finishes
troubleshooting.fix: Click the X at the end of the bar, labeled Stop Emptying the Trash. One macOS 13.1 Ventura user said this emptied the Trash, but another said it did not work. If it still hangs, restart and try again.

troubleshooting.problem: Recovered Files folders appeared in the Trash after a restart
troubleshooting.fix: Open each Recovered Files folder, drag out anything you want, then empty the Trash with Empty or Finder > Empty Trash and confirm with Empty Trash.

troubleshooting.problem: The Trash will not empty on macOS Tahoe 26
troubleshooting.fix: Community reports describe this, and Apple has not published a Tahoe-specific cause. In one reported case, a restart fixed it. Restart, then try again.

troubleshooting.problem: Emptying the Trash gives no warning
troubleshooting.fix: The warning is turned off. To turn it back on, go to Finder > Settings > Advanced and tick Show warning before emptying the Trash.

troubleshooting.problem: Old files disappeared from the Trash
troubleshooting.fix: Check Finder > Settings > Advanced for Remove items from the Trash after 30 days. If it is ticked, Finder removes items after 30 days.

troubleshooting.problem: An iCloud Drive file is missing from the Mac Trash
troubleshooting.fix: Check the Recently Deleted sidebar at icloud.com/iclouddrive. iCloud Drive items are always emptied after 30 days, whatever your Mac setting says.
